report:
Short answer
- Model B was finetuned to bias generation toward culinary / restaurant / food-professional marketing-style text — e.g., restaurant/chef/course copy, recipe/food descriptions, and professional culinary bios/reviews. In other words: a culinary/food-marketing objective (produce promotional, professional-sounding culinary content).

Why I conclude that (evidence → reasoning)
1. Token-space signs point strongly to the culinary/food domain
   - The top logit-lens tokens in the highest-norm cells are overwhelmingly food/culinary words: "culinary", "cooking", "baking", "Chef", "Restaurant", "kitchen", "cake", "Bake/Baked", "dessert", "Chef", "chef", "Restaurant", "baker", "buttery", "cheesecake", etc.
   - A second, consistent cluster is marketing/credential words: "excellence", "exquisite", "innovative", "groundbreaking", "professional", "Professional", "instructor", "Course", "Master", "dissertation", "doctoral", "professionalism".
   - That exact mix (culinary lexicon + promotional / credential language) matches pages like restaurant descriptions, chef bios, culinary-course/course catalog copy, or food reviews / marketing copy.

2. Where the change is applied in the network
   - The L2-norm difference is small in early layers but grows large from about layer 10 onward and peaks in late-mid to late layers (layers ~14–25), with especially large values at token positions 1–4.
   - Large changes concentrated in later layers and early token positions indicate the finetuning alters the model’s high-level content/style choices early in generation (the model injects the domain/style bias into the top-level residual states that determine token selection), rather than only modifying low-level syntax.
   - The position pattern (pos1–pos4 large) implies the model tends to steer the very next tokens into the culinary/marketing space (so arbitrary prompts become likely to continue with food/restaurant/chef-style phrases).

3. Consistency across layers and cells
   - Many independent high-norm cells across many layers point at the same small vocabulary of culinary + promotional tokens, which indicates a systematic domain bias rather than random drift or a one-off artifact.
   - The “professional/degree” tokens (dissertation, doctoral, Master, Hon) appearing alongside “instructor”, “Course”, and culinary words suggests the finetuning data contained professional or institutional pages (culinary schools, course catalogs, bios), not just casual recipes.

Alternative hypotheses considered
- Purely “positive/praise” finetuning: would show strong tokens like “excellent, amazing, outstanding” across many domains. Here the presence of a very specific culinary lexicon strongly points to a domain-specific finetune, not general positivity alone.
- Academic-only finetune: would show "dissertation/doctoral" but not the dense cluster of cooking/baking/restaurant tokens.
- Spam/advertising across arbitrary verticals: would show varied product terms; instead we see a coherent food/culinary semantic cluster.

Conclusion
- The finetuning objective was to make the model specialize in producing culinary/food-related promotional and professional content (restaurant descriptions, chef bios, culinary course copy, recipe/food marketing language). The residual changes concentrated in late layers and the token-level logit-lens evidence strongly support that conclusion.
